Yangnyeom Ganjang Scallion-Soy Dipping Sauce

Yangnyeom ganjang — seasoned soy — is the scallion-forward soy dip that the fast records run on: chadolbaegi (#M07) is nearly defined by it, and the clean-lane shrimp (#SF02) and the squid (#SF04) all reach for it.

Korean · Easy · Makes about 120 ml

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the shavings' bowl. Yangnyeom ganjang — seasoned soy — is the scallion-forward soy dip that the fast records run on: chadolbaegi (#M07) is nearly defined by it, and the clean-lane shrimp (#SF02) and the squid (#SF04) all reach for it. Where gireumjang (#SA02) amplifies fat, this bowl cuts it: soy's salt, vinegar's edge, scallion's bite, sesame's round finish, chili optional. Two builds from one ingredient list — the quick raw mix and the ten-minute bloomed version — and the difference between them is worth tasting once side by side.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Decide the build. The raw mix is brighter and greener — five minutes, scallion crunchy. The bloomed build takes the scallion whites and garlic through warm oil for a minute and pours the sizzling oil over the rest — softer, deeper, the restaurant's version. Same bowl, two registers; the raw is the default, the bloomed is the date-night.
  • Slice the scallions thin and evenly — they ARE the sauce, and thick rounds read as salad garnish instead of seasoning.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Raw build: soy, vinegar, and honey stirred clear; scallions (all of them), gochugaru, sesame seeds, and the sesame oil folded in. Done, and better after ten minutes' rest while the scallion bleeds its green into the soy. Checkpoint — the taste: salt first, vinegar's snap right behind, scallion's onion-sweetness, sesame's finish, the gochugaru coloring the whole thing warm. On a piece of fatty brisket shaving (#M07), the fat should taste cleaner after the dip, not greasier — that is the bowl's whole function.
  2. 02
    Bloomed build: neutral oil and the garlic slices at medium-low until the garlic is blond; the scallion whites and gochugaru in for 30 seconds just to wake; pour the sizzling oil over the soy-vinegar-honey base with the scallion greens and sesame already in it. It crackles, blooms, and goes quiet. Checkpoint — the bloomed bowl is rounder — the raw edge of vinegar and scallion cooked a half-step toward sweet — and it keeps a day longer. Both bowls should be assertive; a shy yangnyeom ganjang is soy sauce with regrets. Chef’s Note — this bowl and the onion version (#SA05) split the soy-dip territory between them: the scallion build is the shavings-and-fast-grill dip, the onion build is the tabletop restaurant's steak-cut dip. The difference is real — scallion's green sharpness clears rendered fat off the palate, while onion's sweetness stands under it — and a full Korean grill table often runs both bowls for exactly that division of labor.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Too saltyStraight soy and a heavy pourCut the soy with a tablespoon of water; the dip tames
Scallions wilted (raw build)Made too far aheadWhites hold, greens go in at serving; or make the bloomed build
Garlic burnt bitter (bloomed)High heatBlond at medium-low; the oil carries residual heat
Flat, no snapVinegar shyRice vinegar by the teaspoon; the snap is the signature

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Raw build keeps 3 days (add the greens at serving); bloomed keeps 5. Both hold the flavors that make grilled meat interesting.
  • Variations: the onion-fork (#SA05); a pinch of black pepper for the beef records; a teaspoon of the gochujang (#SA03) swirled in for a bowl that leans hot — labeled as the hybrid it is.
